extracted.intended_audience: high-school journalism students and beginning student reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing personality (feature) sketches and related student-journalism pieces, plus a linked section on sports reporting technique for student reporters. Emphasizes interview usage, scene/detail, economy, and factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interview-style conversation to reveal personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the personality sketch like an interview: use quoted conversation and exchange to develop the subject’s character and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter repeatedly notes 'How is the sketch like an interview? What is the value of conversation?' and demonstrates sketches in which conversational exchanges, greetings, and answers (often mid-action) reveal character. Stage business and dialog are used to further development; include marginal notes/quotations gathered in interviews and use them to show, not tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with a vivid scene or stage business
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the sketch with stage business or a short scene that immediately illustrates the subject’s character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes and examples show the effect of opening with action (e.g., a man biting into a sandwich, a reporter finding a subject in a secluded corner). The text asks students to 'Note how stage business furthers the development.' Economy of narration means choosing a small vivid scene to stand for larger traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize personality succinctly (lead/summary sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to distill the subject’s personality into a brief, concentrated sentence (exercise: 'In a thirty-word sentence summarize the personality').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercises require producing a compact summary of personality to guide the piece. This functions like a thematic lead or capsule judgment to structure the sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the occasion/context (news peg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain what achievement or occasion has put the person in the public eye; identify the reason for the write-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise: 'What was the occasion of the write-up? In other words, what achievement has put the person described in the public eye?' A personality sketch should connect character detail to a clear occasion or news peg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects with news value (new, strange, picturesque, unexpected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose persons whose stories have news value: the new, the strange, the picturesque, or the unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise advice: 'Remember that the new, the strange, the picturesque, the unexpected have news value.' Keep a list of interesting personalities and notes so you can publish at opportune times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of narration; show with concrete detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice economy: develop the piece with concrete, specific details and omit vague generalities so the sketch reads sharply and efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asks students to 'Note how stage business furthers the development' and 'What instances of economy of narration can you find?' Use concrete description, anecdotes, and selective biography elements rather than long generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include biographical elements selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose which facts from a subject’s background to include — those that illuminate the personality or relate to the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise: 'Select the elements that might be written in the biography of each.' The examples show mixing small personal history (awards, jobs, affiliations) with present action to explain how the person became notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversation and mannerisms to produce adverbs/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: From interviews, extract manner descriptors (adverbs, phrases, gestures) to convey how the subject speaks and moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise tasks: write five adverbs and five phrases showing manner of talking, list gestures and facial expressions—these concrete bits show personality rather than abstract labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep reporting grounded in facts (no vague generalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Base the sketch on observable facts and documented statements rather than speculation or unsupported claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although stated explicitly in the sports section, the instruction 'Whatever the subject of the article, base the discussion on facts. No vague generalities may be used...' applies to all student reporting: write the summary lead and develop by concrete details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get correct identification (names, titles, affiliations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify and report accurate names, positions, titles, affiliations, and relevant factual descriptors for the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout examples, correct naming (e.g., club memberships, offices held) and precise labels (editor-in-chief, correspondent) are used to establish credibility. The sports checklist explicitly requires correct names and positions; the same verification standard holds for personality sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before-the-event sports checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a game, get correct names of players and positions, a list matching uniform numbers to names, and a score card if available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit checklist: '1. Get correct names of players and positions on both teams. If players wear designating numbers, a list giving name and number will facilitate their recognition. Get a score card if available.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Know team records and significance of the game
rubrics_metrics.description: Research previous encounters, each team’s season record, and the significance of the game (intersectional, annual contest, league game, championship implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From sports guidance: 'If the teams are old rivals, get the record of their previous encounters against each other. Get also the record of each team for the current season. Know the significance of the game in the sport calendar.'

rubrics_metrics.name: During-the-game: keep a running account of plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Take continuous notes of plays as they occur to build an accurate play-by-play or summary of key moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction: 'DURING THE GAME: Keep running account of plays.' Decide whether to file play-by-play or focus on important plays depending on space and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: After-the-game: check all data with official scorer
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify statistics, scoring plays, and other recorded data against the official scorer before filing the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction: 'AFTER THE GAME: Check up all data with official scorer’s data.' This ensures accuracy of box scores and reported facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization: lead gives the result; put the news into the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose the article with a lead that states the result (or main news) immediately; the lead should put the news up front.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'ORGANIZATION': 'Proceed as in any news story. The lead, of course, will give the result of the game.' Also repeated rule: 'Put the News Into the Lead.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the vernacular of the game (appropriate sport parlance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the language of the sport (not cheap slang) to add punch and demonstrate knowledge, but avoid partisanship and cheap slang.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'To put punch into sport articles, use the vernacular — not cheap slang — but the language of the game, the language that lovers of the game understand.' Distinguish baseball parlance from football parlance, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide story type: play-by-play vs. feature/box
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether to file a play-by-play account or to focus on a feature/analysis about the game; side plays may suggest separate box features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: 'The reporter will have to decide whether to turn in a play-by-play report (usually space permits a report of important plays only) or whether to play up some feature of the game. In any case the reader wants facts.' Side plays can be turned into box features or longer features apart from the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate comment/opinion from the game report
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix editorial comment or partisan opinion into the game report; place commentary in editorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions: 'If comment is desirable, put it into an editorial. True, you may find comment in sports articles in the daily press, but the practice is not one to be imitated by the high school journalist.' Also the CAUTION: 'No opinions! No comment! No dope! No partisanship!'

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow standard forms for summaries, line-ups and box scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the format established on the sport page of a good daily newspaper or your publication’s style sheet for summaries, line-ups, and box scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: 'For summaries, line-ups, and box scores, follow the form used on the sport page of a good daily newspaper unless your style sheet gives the form to use.' Study professional examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report other sports news with a factual summary lead and concrete details
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering non-game sports topics (team future, coaching changes, practice introduced), base discussion on facts and use a summary lead developed with concrete details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'REPORTING OTHER SPORT NEWS: Besides the report of games, sport writers may want to write up other sport news... Whatever the subject of the article, base the discussion on facts. ... Write the summary lead and develop by concrete details.'
